::: {.finding}
The bracket shows where the middle 80% of Minnesota elementary schools land, and all of it sits below the line. Nine of 833 schools have a fifth grade average above 550. A third of fifth graders score in the ten points just beneath it.

### Beyond Proficient

::: {.meta}
Science MCA-IV, spring 2025. Grades 5, 8, and high school.
:::

Minnesota reports school science performance as a percent proficient. That number turns out to be almost entirely determined by two things the state also publishes: a school's average score and how spread out its scores are. Which means proficiency rates exaggerate real differences. Two schools nine scale points apart report 17% and 43%.

[See the analysis and dashboard](projects/beyond-proficient/index.qmd){.view}
:::

### MnCOSE 2026

::: {.meta}
What, How, Why. Minnesota Conference on Science Education, November 2026.
:::

A classroom routine that moves students from labeled diagrams to models that explain. Students ask what they can see, how it happens underneath, and why it works, then revise one model three times across a unit. Presented to science teachers and district leaders from across Minnesota.

[See the session](projects/mncose-2026/index.qmd){.view}
:::
:::

### Minnesota Early Learning Scholarships

::: {.meta}
County-level awards across five fiscal years.
:::

Minnesota publishes scholarship awards by county but not the rate at which awarded scholarships go unused. Deriving that rate showed which counties are most exposed when a large one-time appropriation runs out.

[See the analysis and dashboard](projects/early-learning/index.qmd){.view}
:::
:::

## How I work

When two test series are not comparable, I do not draw a trend line across them, even when the chart would look better for it.

Science MCA-IV replaced MCA-III in 2025 against a different set of standards. There is no valid multi-year science trend in Minnesota right now, and saying that plainly is more useful than pointing at something adjacent. The same goes for suppressed cells, which get counted rather than quietly dropped, and for measures I derive myself, which get labeled as derived.

The reason to be careful about any of this is that teachers have to make decisions with these numbers. A clear picture of what the data supports is worth more to them than a confident one.
